content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the task of unsupervised scene decomposition. The authors propose to solve this task by applying normalizing flows, by representing the scene as a mixture of bidirectional flows. Quantitative results show comparable performance on the synthetic CLEVR dataset and Real-Traffic's real-world image dataset compared to the state-of-the-art.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- It is interesting to see the application of normalizing flow to the task of unsupervised scene decomposition. The proposed method also shows good results on real image datasets.

- I see the authors do their best to describe how the mixing of bidirectional streams is formulated and how it can be applied algorithmically to the task of unsupervised scene decomposition.

Weaknesses:
- I think the presentation of the paper could be further refined. For example, Figures 3 and 4 seem a bit redundant to illustrate the dataset labels themselves. It is better to provide qualitative results directly comparing to state-of-the-art methods on each dataset respectively.

- It's also better to show runtime comparison (including training and inference times) against the state-of-the-art methods. I do see better performance on real data by using normalizing flows, however, I also wonder if this introduces more computational cost.

- It would be good to discuss in further detail why the proposed method does not perform well on synthetic datasets. Is it because the model is overfitting the simple background and foreground? Qualitative comparisons can be a good indicator. The authors claim that the real image dataset is more challenging, but the image background shown in Figures 4 and 5 is not complicated as it is also mostly untextured roads with a few lanes. Also, cars show similar shapes, which should be less challenging compared to synthetic datasets containing objects of different shapes. I think the authors need to dig into this to explain the mechanism and root cause. Otherwise, I feel that NF is overfitting the dataset with simple background textures and similar object shapes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the presentation (clarification and quality) of the paper needs further improvement.
There are some novel points, such as introducing bi-directional flow of foreground objects and background into the task of unsupervised scene decomposition, but I am not clear on the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I appreciate the author's efforts in introducing NF to new tasks. I also appreciate the effort to evaluate on real image datasets. However, I think the presentation of the paper needs further refinement and lacks many explanations and illustrations, including qualitative comparisons and root causes, such as the different performance on synthetic and real image data. Therefore, I vote for borderline reject.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript explores the problem of unsupervised scene decomposition using invertible coupling layers introduced by the real NVP paper. An image is mapped to background and foreground vectors. The background is trained without using background-only images because in a batch there usually exists one image that the background is visible at a certain pixel. The foreground is further disentangled into location, scale, presence and fg/bg. The key technique is to apply a spatial transformer on these channels as a regularization, but I fail to understand it. Evaluations are done on CLEVR and real-world road scene dataset, showing comparable or better performance than applicable baselines. Codes are not promised or provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The idea of using invertible layers to decompose an image in an unsupervised manner is new and interesting to me.

Weaknesses:
- The first major issue is a lack of clarity about the disentanglement regularization loss. I fail to understand why the spatial transformer can be used in a pixel-wise manner. Three possibilities: (1) every pixel corresponds to a set of transformation parameters. In this case, we don't need a spatial transformer right? (2) every instance gets a set of transformation parameters. Seems impossible as the method cannot distinguish instances; (3) the whole image gets a set of transformation parameters. Seems not applicable too. All in all, I cannot understand this part and please kindly correct me if I am wrong.
- Lack of editing power. Evaluations are only done using the reconstruction metric. And I think the method cannot be used for editing as instances are not distinguishable. So what kind of decomposition are we pursuing? How about changing the location and scale map for re-synthesis?
- I think the road scene is not convincing enough. Please consider using the dataset and evaluation protocols of [A], which allows editing.

[A] Neural scene graphs for dynamic scenes, CVPR 2021

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper uses normalizing flows to learn unsupervised, object-centric representations of scenes. A model learns a distribution over images that is structured, with distinct components for the scene background and (potentially) different foreground objects. Each foreground latent is decoded via reversible mappings into sub-latents that determine an object's presence, position, scale, and appearance. Thus the decoding of these distributions results in a structured decomposition of the encoded image. This normalizing flow-based model is compared to a number of other generative models that have been used for unsupervised scene decomposition.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper provides an extensive review of the literature on generative models for unsupervised scene decomposition and their differences. However, it does not provide a strong rationale for why normalizing flows are a better tool for learning scene decomposition than other approaches. 

Furthermore, the experimental tests of this idea/model are extremely limited. CLEVR has now been used for several years as a simple synthetic benchmark of unsupervised segmentation, and performance appears to be saturated -- many models solve it essentially perfectly (at least according to the ARI metric.) Thus, CLEVR is no longer diagnostic for whether an unsupervised scene decomposition model is improving the state-of-the-art -- especially on challenging, diverse, real-world datasets on which unsupervised segmentation is now possible (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14294, https://www.ecva.net/papers/eccv_2022/papers_ECCV/papers/136890708.pdf, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12181.)

In light of these advances in unsupervised segmentation on much more challenging real-world datasets (more challenging than the relatively homogeneous traffic scenes used here, as well), a new unsupervised object discovery method needs to be justified either by improved results in these harder settings or by some critical qualitative property that other approaches lack (e.g. an ability to manipulate or generate counterfactual scenes.)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written clearly. However, the justification in the introduction for using normalizing flows is not very persuasive -- the main problems with comparable approaches are not minor details about producing background clutter or failing on large numbers of objects, but rather that they simply do not work on complex, real-world scenes. The use of normalizing flows on this task may be novel (though there are so many methods that it's hard to keep track of them all) -- but the novelty does not seem to address a particularly well-defined problem, nor does it result in a large improvement relative to more recent methods.
content.summary_of_the_review: Normalizing flows may be fine as a technique for decomposing simple synthetic scenes -- at least en par with some other well-known methods -- but this setting is outdated. There are now methods that can decompose complex, real-world scenes without supervision, and this is where performance improvements or useful qualitative properties need to be demonstrated to make such work compelling.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work studies the task of scene decomposition: given a dataset of RGB images of a particular scene and variable layouts, we seek to learn it decomposition, i.e. obtain the model which is able to locate and manipulate the objects on it. Authors develop a framework for this task based on normalizing flows, where they construct a mapping between images and it decomposed representation. The model is trained end-to-end in an almost unsupervised manner.  The authors show 4 experiments for it: 2 full launches on CLEVR6 and Real-Traffic data at the 128x128 resolution + 2 ablations for CLEVR.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The authors constructed an interesting framework, managing to combine non-trivial components together (normalizing flows, spatial transformer, gumbel softmax) in a way that works in practice. I believe that those components could be borrowed by subsequent projects for other tasks as well.
2. The method looks simpler than the analogs, while having both generative and discriminative capabilities.
3. The method should be faster and more stable to train than the existing GAN-based setups.

Weaknesses:
1. Missing experiments: how does the method work on a dataset with variable background (e.g. ShapeStacks from RELATE)? 
2. The method works in 2D, while many contemporary frameworks switched to 3D. While it's not a problem on its own, the paper somewhat neglects this difference while comparing to them. For example, it makes statements that it is fast at train/inference time, while NeRF-based ones are slow. This does not look like a big advantage, considering that the NeRF-based models operate in 3D space instead. 
3. It's not clear how the method will perform if we do not know the correct prior for the scale from Table 5. Could you provide some ablations?
4. The method is based on normalizing flows, which do not scale well (i.e. Glow uses a lot of compute, while not achieving SotA quality).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- *Clarity*. I didn't have any issues of following the paper, except for Sec 3.1.4, but it is in general more technically involved, so it's not a big issue.
- *Quality*. My main concern is about the empirical evaluation. It would be interesting to see how it performs on a dataset with variable backgrounds and how robust the method when we do not know the GT prior distributions for the scale (from Table 5).
- *Novelty*. It is good in terms of novelty (to the best of my knowledge).
- *Reproducibility*. The paper seems to provide quite a lot of details to get reproduced. But it's difficult to state this for sure until you actually start reproducing it. So releasing the source code would help in this regard.
content.summary_of_the_review: I find the overall idea to be novel and good, but have the concerns about the empirical evaluation: it is not clear how the method will perform on more challenging datasets with variable background (e.g., ShapeStacks or Real-Car from RELATE/BlockGAN) and how it will perform in a completely unsupervised setting (when we do not know even the parameters for the prior distribution for scales).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
DeNF proposes a flow based (hence invertible) generative model with a foreground background separated latent space, where the foreground is further decomposed spatially through grid cells into presence (binary segmentation of foreground), location, scale and attribute (following Attend, Infer, Repeat, Eslami et al. and could be seen as YOLO inspired parametrization of detection) latent codes. 

Using the forward flow maps the image to these latent variables with different base distributions that are enforced during training. The authors additionally train both the foreground and background component with a backward flow i.e. sampling back the foreground and background (they are sampled independently, instead of jointly. While sampling the foreground image, the background latent is forced to 0s i.e. the mean of the distribution and vice versa. The two are layered together using $z_{pres}$ to get the final reconstructed image) from the inferred latents and enforcing image space losses. Additionally to enforce consistency, the authors use $z_{loc}$ and $z_{scale}$ along with a spatial transformer to compose a foreground segmentation map, which is enforced to be consistent with $z_{pres}$, which is the foreground/background bernoulli random variable during training. 

The authors experiment on CLEVR-6 (a subset of CLEVR with maximum 6 objects) and the Real-Traffic dataset (5 hours of footage from a single fixed traffic camera) and show that they obtain competitive, but worse segmentation performance to baselines on CLEVR-6 and better FID than some previous methods on the Real-Traffic dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
- The motivation to propose an invertible model for higher correlation between decomposition and image generation compared to VAE and GAN based approaches is sound
- The consistency loss between $z_{pres}$ and $z_{loc}, z_{scale}$ is clever. Having $z_{loc}$ and $z_{scale}$ allows decoding boxes in YOLO style and applying non maximum suppression to show unsupervised detected bounding boxes from the method

# Weaknesses

- I believe that the proposed method would not scale to scenes with diverse backgrounds. In fact, the authors take advantange of the fact that the two datasets they show results on have the exact same background in all scenes during training. The authors consistently mention the need for scalability and that competing methods use simplistic datasets for scene generation. However, the datasets used in the paper itself are very simple and the authors use the fact that they have consistent backgrounds in training. Points below:

When training the backward flow for the background (i.e. to have an image space loss on the background), the authors reconstruct backgrounds by adding small noise to the latent and compare one pixel in one reconstruction to every other pixel in the same location across the batch and use the minimum discrepancy as the loss. This uses the fact that with multiple images in the batch (with the same background), there is a high probability that one of the images has a background pixel. 

When training the backward flow for the foreground, the authors compose the scene using indepdently generated foreground and background. The background used is the perturbed background generated for the point above (i.e. by adding small noise to the forward encoded latent in the flow). Afterwards, a L2 reconstruction loss is used. Is this a sensible decision? If the dataset did not have consistent backgrounds, one would expect adding some noise to the encoded background latent to generate a novel background image. Using the novel background image in an L2 reconstruction loss should not provide a meaningful signal? 
\end{itemized}

- How is $z_{what}$ for the background used? $z_{what}$ is split into two distributions conditional on $z_{pres} =$ 0 or 1 but during the foreground generation, only the foreground aspect is used, as it should be. But, why was $z_{what}$ for the background needed in the first place? The authors show experimentally that using a bimodal prior for $z_{what}$ improves ARI on CLEVR6 -- I would appreciate an explanation for this and would also love to be pointed to how the background mode of $z_{what}$ is used in the paper, perhaps I missed this.

- In general, the experiment section of the paper is lacking significantly. IODINE (Greff et al.) for example provide significant analysis of the method, including failure modes, analysis on many datasets including challenging datasets where the model fails as well as analysis on the stability of representations under ambiguous input. This paper only measures FID on the real-traffic dataset and ARI for segmentation on CLEVR-6, which is already a saturated benchmark. Real-traffic was used in Ehrhardt et al. for video generation, where it makes much more sense to be able to disentangle dynamics of various (sometimes overlapping) objects. 

- The only ablation studies are the use of bimodel vs. unimodal prior for $z_{what}$ which itself is unclear as mentioned above and the spatial dimension of the latent variables, which hardly uncover any non-trivial understanding of the proposed method

- It is unclear how overlapping objects are dealt with in the model. There is a $min$ operation used in the consistency loss where overlapping contributions from $z_{loc}$ and $z_{scale}$ are clamped to a max of 1. How does this affect gradient dynamics? Would it make sense to softly clamp to the 0,1 range instead?

- How is FID computed for Real-Traffic? From the text, it is quite unclear. From the text in section 4.1, it seems that the authors encode a test scene into latents and then sample from the predicted distribution to generate new scenes. If that is indeed true, this is conditional sampling. Is conditional sampling the appropriate way of sampling from the generative model and computing FID? The same table lists DCGAN as a baseline. How was sampling done for DCGAN? Was it unconditional as one would expect or was it made conditional somehow?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is clear regarding the formulation
- I believe the idea of using structured priors in a normalizing flow framework to decompose scenes is novel
- There are clarity issues in the paper, especially in experiments that are mentioned above.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the idea is novel and interesting. However, in its current form I believe the idea over-relies on the presence of consistent backgrounds in the datasets. Moreover, the experiment section is significantly lacking and provides little insight into how and why the model works. The FID computation for the Real-Traffic data is unclear. There are strong claims regarding scalability and fidelity in the paper that are not backed by experiments. Due to these, I cannot recommend accept at this time. I would recommend that the authors experiment on a more complex scene dataset, such as LSUN-Bedrooms (used by BlobGAN, Epstein et al.) to show scalability to diverse backgrounds. I would also recommend the authors to work on their formulation further to remove the need for datasets with consistent backgrounds from the method.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
